chapters.title: 2 Timothy 3:16: ‘All Scripture Is God-Breathed’ or ‘Every God-Breathed Scripture’?
chapters.subtitle: One verse, no verb, and two honest ways to translate it
chapters.nutshell: Paul’s Greek sentence in 2 Timothy 3:16 has no verb, so every translator must decide where to put “is”. Most versions read “All Scripture is God-breathed and useful”; some older ones read “Every God-breathed Scripture is also useful”. Both are possible Greek, and both say that Scripture comes from God and equips his people.
chapters.bigIdea: Whichever way the verse is read, Scripture is breathed out by God and given to make his people ready for every good work.
skeleton: The Greek has no verb: translators must supply “is”
Reading A: “All Scripture is God-breathed and useful”
Reading B: “Every God-breathed Scripture is also useful”
Grammar and context lean towards A, but B is possible
For Timothy, “Scripture” meant the sacred writings of Israel
Either way: from God, and useful to equip

p: Greek often leaves out the little verb “is”, and the reader fills it in. 2 Timothy 3:16 begins with four words and no verb: πᾶσα γραφὴ θεόπνευστος καὶ ὠφέλιμος — “all/every scripture God-breathed and useful”. Then comes the list: for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training in righteousness.

Where the translator puts “is” changes the shape of the sentence. This is not a matter of hidden motives; it is simply what happens when a verbless Greek sentence must become a full English (or Tamil) one.

Reading A puts “is” after “Scripture”: “All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful.” Here both words — God-breathed and useful — are things said about Scripture. The KJV, NIV, ESV, NASB and RSV read it this way.

Reading B puts “is” after “God-breathed”: “Every God-breathed Scripture is also useful.” Here “God-breathed” describes Scripture, and the main statement is that it is useful. The Latin Vulgate, Tyndale, the English Revised Version (1881), the American Standard Version (1901) and the NEB read it this way.

When two adjectives are joined by καί (“and”), the most natural reading is that both are said about the noun in the same way. A close parallel is 1 Timothy 4:4: “every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected.” This favours Reading A.

Reading B must take καί to mean “also” (“is also useful”). Greek can do that, but it is less natural here. πᾶσα without the article can mean “every” (each passage of Scripture) or “all” (Scripture as a whole); either fits both readings.
θεόπνευστος (theopneustos) joins θεός, “God”, and a form of πνέω, “to breathe”: literally “God-breathed”. This verse is the earliest known use of the word anywhere in Greek.

It recalls the picture of God’s breath giving life (Genesis 2:7) and creating by his word (Psalm 33:6). The English “inspired” comes from the Latin inspirata, “breathed into”; the Greek stresses that Scripture comes out from God’s own breath, which is why the ESV says “breathed out by God”.

The verse before speaks of “the sacred writings” (ἱερὰ γράμματα) that Timothy had known “from childhood” (3:15), taught by his mother and grandmother (1:5). That means the Hebrew Bible — the Law, the Prophets and the Writings — which Jews of the Greek-speaking world often read in the Greek Septuagint.

The context stresses purpose: Scripture makes wise for salvation (3:15) and makes the person of God “complete, equipped for every good work” (3:17). Paul’s point is what Scripture does, because of where it comes from.

Both readings are grammatically possible. Most modern scholars and translations prefer Reading A, mainly because of the natural force of καί and parallels like 1 Timothy 4:4. The Tamil Union Version also follows A: “வேதவாக்கியங்களெல்லாம் தேவஆவியினால் அருளப்பட்டிருக்கிறது” (wording approximate).

Reading B does not mean that some Scripture is not inspired. It describes Scripture as God-breathed and then says it is also useful. Either way the verse teaches the same two things: Scripture comes from God, and it is given to teach, correct and equip.

keyPoints: The Greek of 2 Timothy 3:16 has no verb; every translation must supply “is”.
Reading A: “All Scripture is God-breathed and useful” (KJV, NIV, ESV).
Reading B: “Every God-breathed Scripture is also useful” (Vulgate, RV, ASV, NEB).
The grammar (καί joining two adjectives) and parallels like 1 Timothy 4:4 make A the more natural reading.
Either way, Scripture comes from God and is given to teach and equip; B does not imply that some Scripture is uninspired.
reflect: Does it change how you read your Bible to know that translators sometimes must choose between two honest options?
Paul links God-breathed Scripture with being equipped for good works. Which good work is Scripture preparing you for now?

quiz.q: Why must translators add a word to 2 Timothy 3:16?
options: The Greek sentence has no verb
A word was lost from the manuscripts
quiz.why: The Greek simply says “all/every scripture God-breathed and useful”; “is” must be supplied.

quiz.q: Which version follows Reading B (“Every scripture inspired of God is also profitable”)?
quiz.why: The RV of 1881 and the ASV of 1901 chose Reading B.
It joins “God” and “breathe”; this verse is its earliest known use.

quiz.q: Which statement is a fair conclusion?
options: Only Reading B is possible Greek
Reading B means some Scripture is not inspired
The verse is about the New Testament only
Both readings are possible, and both say Scripture comes from God and is useful
quiz.why: Most scholars prefer A, but both teach Scripture’s divine origin and usefulness.

chapters.title: Isaiah 53:10: Why the Septuagint Reads Differently
chapters.subtitle: Crushed or cleansed? How one verse reached us in different ancient forms
chapters.nutshell: In the Hebrew text, Isaiah 53:10 says it was the LORD’s will “to crush” his servant; in the Greek Septuagint, the Lord wishes “to cleanse him from the blow”. Ancient copies and translations differ here because of an unclear Hebrew verse, translators’ choices and interpretation. Seeing why helps us read Isaiah 53 — and its use in the New Testament — more carefully.
chapters.bigIdea: The ancient witnesses to Isaiah 53 differ in wording, but together they show how early readers heard the servant’s suffering as purifying and life-giving.
skeleton: Hebrew (MT): the LORD willed to crush him; a guilt offering; he will see offspring
Greek (LXX): the Lord wishes to cleanse him; if you give an offering for sin
The Targum: the LORD’s will to refine and purify; applied to the Messiah
The Dead Sea scroll and LXX: “he will see light” in 53:11
How the New Testament reads Isaiah 53

p: The standard Hebrew text (the Masoretic Text, MT) of Isaiah 53:10 reads roughly: “Yet it was the LORD’s will to crush him; he made him sick; if (or when) his soul makes a guilt offering (asham), he will see offspring, he will prolong his days.”

The Greek Septuagint (LXX), translated in Alexandria about the 2nd century BC, reads: “And the Lord wishes to cleanse him from the blow; if you give an offering for sin, your soul will see long-lived offspring.” Same verse — but a very different picture.

1) “Crush” vs “cleanse”: the Hebrew דַּכְּאוֹ comes from דכא, “crush”. One explanation, widely suggested, is that the translator read it in the light of the Aramaic root דכי, “to be clean, pure”. 2) “He made him sick” (הֶחֱלִי) vs “from the blow”: the translator may have read the word as a noun, “the sickness”.

3) תָּשִׂים can mean “you make” or “she makes” (nefesh, “soul”, is feminine — so “his soul makes”). The LXX chose “if you (plural) give”, addressing the people. 4) asham, a “guilt offering” (Leviticus 5), becomes simply “for sin”.

sections.h: The Targum and the Dead Sea scroll
p: The Aramaic Targum of Isaiah, read in synagogues, paraphrases freely. In 53:10 it speaks of the LORD’s will “to refine and to purify” (wording approximate), applying it to the remnant of his people, and it names the servant as “my servant the Messiah” (52:13).

In 53:11 the Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran (1QIsaᵃ, about 125 BC) and the LXX both say “he will see light”. The word “light” is not in the MT. This shows that some Hebrew copies older than the MT had a slightly different text.

Translators worked from the Hebrew copy in front of them (their Vorlage), which was not always identical to the later MT. They also made choices where the Hebrew is hard — and Isaiah 53:10 is one of the most difficult verses in the book. Finally, every translation is also an interpretation: the LXX and the Targum show how Jewish readers of their day understood the servant.
None of this means that someone tampered with the Bible. It is the normal life of an ancient text copied and translated by hand over many centuries.

sections.h: How the New Testament reads Isaiah 53
p: The apostles saw Jesus in Isaiah 53. Philip explains Isaiah 53:7–8 to the Ethiopian official, quoted in its Greek form (Acts 8:32–35). Peter weaves 53:4–9 into his words on Christ’s suffering (1 Peter 2:22–25). Matthew applies 53:4 to Jesus’ healings, in wording closer to the Hebrew (Matthew 8:17).
So the NT writers used both Greek and Hebrew forms of Isaiah, choosing the wording that best served their teaching.

The Greek and Aramaic readings do not settle what the Hebrew means, and the Hebrew “crush” must be taken seriously. But they show that early Jewish readers heard this passage in terms of cleansing and purification, not only of punishment.

That fits a wider biblical theme taught elsewhere in this app: sacrifice is about cleansing and restoring (Leviticus 16:30; Hebrews 9:14) rather than appeasing an angry God. Read gently, Isaiah 53 holds both: the servant truly suffers, and through it many are made clean and righteous (53:11).

verses.text: Yet it pleased the LORD to bruise him; he hath put him to grief: when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed.
He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities… and with his stripes we are healed.
He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied: by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many.
Then Philip opened his mouth, and began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus.
Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree… by whose stripes ye were healed.

keyPoints: The Hebrew of Isaiah 53:10 says the LORD willed “to crush” his servant; the Septuagint says “to cleanse him from the blow”.
One widely suggested explanation: the translator read the Hebrew in the light of an Aramaic root meaning “to be pure”.
The Targum speaks of refining and purifying and applies the passage to the Messiah and the people.
The Great Isaiah Scroll and the LXX add “light” in 53:11, showing that Hebrew copies once differed slightly.
Different copies, hard Hebrew and interpretation explain the differences — not tampering.
reflect: How does it help you to know that early readers heard Isaiah 53 in terms of cleansing as well as suffering?
Philip began “at the same scripture” and preached Jesus. How would you explain Isaiah 53 to someone today?

quiz.q: What does the Septuagint say in Isaiah 53:10 where the Hebrew says “to crush him”?
options: To cleanse him from the blow
quiz.why: The LXX reads καθαρίσαι αὐτὸν ἀπὸ τῆς πληγῆς, “to cleanse him from the blow”.

quiz.q: Which word is found in 1QIsaᵃ and the LXX of Isaiah 53:11 but not in the MT?
quiz.why: Both read “he will see light” (LXX: “to show him light”).

quiz.q: Why can תָּשִׂים be translated in two ways?
options: It can mean “you make” or “she (his soul) makes”
It was added by the Masoretes
quiz.why: The same Hebrew form serves for “you” (masc.) and “she”; nefesh (soul) is feminine.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a reason ancient texts of Isaiah differ?
quiz.why: The differences come from copies, difficulty and interpretation — the normal history of a text.
